# 6. Archetypes {#sec-archetypes}

The recurring resolutions — combinations of competing pressures settled at a particular scale zone and sharing position that keep reappearing across real projects. Archetypes are the **structure register**: what the two axes (scale × sharing–sparing) produce, paired with the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) that overlay them. We use *archetype* in its plain sense — a characteristic, recurring, transformable pattern, not an exhaustive set.

**Overhead and interspace — the two hardware types beneath the archetypes.** The field's engineering standards (DIN SPEC 91434; the NREL / InSPIRE configuration taxonomy) sort agrivoltaic hardware into **overhead** systems — modules elevated *above* the working surface, the vegetable-agrivoltaics case — and **interspace** systems — modules mounted low with the crop or cover *between* the rows, the vertical-bifacial and grazing cases. That typology classifies the *structure*; the archetypes here classify the *resolution of pressures*. The two registers are complementary, not rival: one structural class can appear in several archetypes, and one archetype can be built in more than one class.

This chapter develops **six featured archetypes** in depth — each with its pressures, its internal variation, and a worked real-world application — then reads them across the [SCALE domains](#sec-archetype-domains), and closes with **seven further archetypes** in current circulation. They are ordered along the [scale transect](1-the-scale-transect.qmd), from the farmstead yard to the region. That they happen to cover it is a result, not a selection rule: an archetype is featured here because it recurs in the field and carries at least one documented case, and the mid scales hold the most because that is where the freedom to choose the ground and the freedom to manage it overlap. A form that looks promising but is not yet documented as recurring belongs among the further archetypes, marked as emerging — the set is meant to grow and be corrected, not to fill a diagram. Each archetype states its *dominant* and *yielded* pressures; read across the domains, those trade-offs become a characteristic footprint that distinguishes one archetype from another.

## What appears at each scale {#sec-by-zone}

If you know roughly how much land is in play, start here. The table gives the forms that recur at each [zone](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) — **featured archetypes in bold**, [further ones](#sec-further-types) in plain text — and each name links to its entry. Arrays mounted on buildings take no ground at all and sit at [A0](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones), off the table entirely.

::: {.zone-table}
| Zone | Indicative footprint | Forms that recur here |
|---|---|---|
| **A1 — Farmstead** | under ~1 acre | [**Barnyard Shelter**](#arch-barnyard) |
| **A2 — Field** | ~0.5–8 acres | [**Vegetable Agrivoltaics**](#arch-vegetable) · [**Marginal Land**](#arch-marginal) · [Vertical-Bifacial Cropland](#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [Recharge Enhancement](#arch-recharge) |
| **A3 — Parcel** | ~5–80 acres | [**Solar Prairie Strips**](#arch-prairie-strips) · [**Vegetable Agrivoltaics**](#arch-vegetable) · [**Marginal Land**](#arch-marginal) · [Community-Solar Pollinator](#arch-community-solar) · [Vertical-Bifacial Cropland](#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [Recharge Enhancement](#arch-recharge) · [Linear Infrastructure](#arch-linear) · [Ag-Industrial Microgrid](#arch-microgrid) · [Brightfield](#arch-brightfield) |
| **A4 — Landscape** | ~60–400 acres | [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](#arch-grazing) · [**Water-Sustainability**](#arch-water) · [Native-Grassland Utility](#arch-native-grassland) · [Vertical-Bifacial Cropland](#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [Linear Infrastructure](#arch-linear) · [Ag-Industrial Microgrid](#arch-microgrid) · [Brightfield](#arch-brightfield) |
| **A5 — Regional** | ~300 acres to 10,000+ | [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](#arch-grazing) · [**Water-Sustainability**](#arch-water) · [Native-Grassland Utility](#arch-native-grassland) · [Brightfield](#arch-brightfield) |
:::

**Read the crowding.** A3 (Parcel) carries the most forms and A1 and A5 the fewest — which is the [feasible wedge](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-wedge) (§2.2) appearing in a table built for an entirely different purpose. Mid-scale is where the freedom to choose the ground and the freedom to manage it overlap, so it holds the most distinct answers; the ends narrow because one freedom or the other runs out. Scale narrows the menu before design begins — that is the whole argument of §1, arriving here as a practical fact.

**A caution about reading down a column.** A form appearing at your zone means it *has been built* at that scale, not that it suits your site. Climate, soil, water, market, and what the neighbours will accept all cut the list further, and several of these forms are mutually exclusive on the same ground. The entries below say what each one demands.

## The six featured archetypes {#sec-featured}

**On the worked cases.** Each featured archetype carries one real project. Several rest on developer pages, NGO case studies, and extension write-ups rather than peer-reviewed evidence; capacities and areas are as-reported and are traced in [Sources](sources.qmd). They illustrate the *form* — they are not verified performance data, and none of them has been independently audited against the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) it is cited for.


### Barnyard Shelter Solar {#arch-barnyard}


::: {.at-a-glance}
**At a glance** — *indicative: drawn from the worked case and from forms in circulation. Not requirements.*

- **Scale** — A1 · ~10–100 kW · under about an acre
- **Position** — S1–S2 — the farm's own animals keep using the ground beneath
- **Ground layer** — the existing yard or paddock; nothing new to establish
- **Clearance** — enough for stock to walk in and shelter under (the case below: cows)
- **Grid** — behind-the-meter — offsets the parlour, cold store, well pump
- **Watch for** — muck and wear concentrating where the animals crowd into the shade
:::
*Farmstead scale [A1](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · shares the ground with the farm's own animals [S1–S2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) · restoration by how it's run*

Barnyard shelter solar has two layers that keep each other's company: the farm's own animals — a dairy herd, a few beef cows, a flock of hens — and a modest array raised over the yard or paddock where they already gather. The panels are shelter first and generation second: shade in the heat of the afternoon, a dry place out of the rain, a break from the wind, and for poultry a roof against the hawk. The same structure quietly runs the milking parlour, the cold store, the well pump — the farm's own power, drawn off its own meter.

This is the smallest archetype and the most fully the farmer's own. One person holds the animals, the panels, and the labour, and can set the array exactly where the herd stands on a July afternoon — no lease, no contractor, no grid study, every lever in a single pair of hands. The reward is read in the animals as much as the meter: shaded dairy cows run a degree cooler and pant less through the worst of the heat, and hens with cover overhead range farther from the coop. The catch is simply scale — a few tens of kilowatts offset a farm, not a county — and the shade that draws the herd also concentrates it, so the muck and the wear gather where the animals crowd beneath the panels.

*Dominant pressures: agricultural continuity, operational simplicity. Yielded: generation at scale — the array is sized to the farm, not the grid.*

**West Central Research and Outreach Center, Morris, Minnesota** — a University of Minnesota dairy where a 30-kilowatt array was raised over the pasture in 2018 to shade thirty to forty grazing cows and power the milking equipment; the shaded herd ran about a degree cooler and panted less, while the same panels carried the parlour's load — a working demonstration that shelter and generation can sit together on one small farm.

### Vegetable Agrivoltaics {#arch-vegetable}


::: {.at-a-glance}
**At a glance** — *indicative: drawn from the worked case and from forms in circulation. Not requirements.*

- **Scale** — A2–A3 · ~100 kW–3 MW · roughly 1–20 acres
- **Position** — S1 — the food crop continues inside the footprint
- **Ground layer** — shade-tolerant vegetables — greens, tomatoes, peppers
- **Geometry** — clearance for hand and small-equipment work; row spacing set by the crop's light needs, not by packing density
- **Grid** — behind-the-meter to distribution
- **Watch for** — shade past the crop's tolerance — the most engineering-intensive form here, and the one most sensitive to climate
:::
*Field scale [A2–A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · shares the ground for food [S1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) · restoration by how it's built*

Vegetable agrivoltaics has two layers that share the same ground: a food crop below — greens, tomatoes, peppers, the shade-tolerant vegetables — and solar panels above, raised and spaced so that enough light still reaches the rows. The crop keeps the land in production; the panels add power and a second income, and in hot, dry country their shade is not a cost but a gift, cutting the heat and water stress on the plants beneath.

Everything turns on light. The panels sit high enough to work under and far enough apart, or clear enough, to leave the crop what it needs — which makes this the most engineering-intensive archetype, its geometry tuned to a particular plant in a particular climate. Push the shade too far and yield falls; get it right somewhere like the desert Southwest and the same panels that make electricity also make the afternoon survivable for a tomato [@barrongafford2019]. It stays small, close to the farmer, and it lives or dies on whether the crop underneath still pays.

*Dominant pressures: agricultural continuity, social license. Yielded: some generation and capital, to the clearance and spacing the crop demands.*

**Jack's Solar Garden, Colorado** — the largest commercial agrivoltaics research site in the country: 1.2 megawatts of tracking panels over four acres where partner farmers grow chard, greens, and tomatoes among the rows, a living laboratory for NREL, Colorado State, and University of Arizona researchers.

### Marginal Land Solar {#arch-marginal}


::: {.at-a-glance}
**At a glance** — *indicative: drawn from the worked case and from forms in circulation. Not requirements.*

- **Scale** — A2–A3 · ~100 kW–3 MW · roughly 1–20 acres
- **Position** — S4 — or S2 where the ground still carries stock
- **Ground layer** — whatever the marginal ground supports: rough grazing where it drains, naturalized or pollinator cover where it does not
- **Geometry** — dictated by the parcel — orientation and layout follow the ground, not the optimum
- **Grid** — behind-meter to distribution; the interconnect run can be long
- **Watch for** — ground that is marginal for farming is often marginal for solar too — ballast on rock, elevation above a floodplain, extra cable
:::
*Field to parcel scale [A2–A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · spares by taking idled ground [S4](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) — [S2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) where that ground still grazes · restoration by where you site*

Marginal land solar has two layers only loosely joined: a patch of ground the farm had all but given up on — a flood-prone corner, a rocky headland, a wet or oddly-shaped remnant that never paid its way — and an array set on it, turning idle acres into a second income without touching the good fields. Whatever the ground can still carry comes along underneath: rough grazing where it drains, naturalized or pollinator cover where it does not.

The defining choice is made before anyone thinks about output — it is a decision about *which* ground, not how to wring watts from it — and the array simply accepts the orientation and layout the site dictates. That is also the catch: land that was marginal for farming is often marginal for solar too, awkwardly shaped or oriented, sometimes needing costly answers — ballast on rock, elevation above a floodplain, a longer run to the interconnection. It works when the new income clears that penalty, and like the prairie strips it leans on the mid-scale freedom to choose the parcel; assemble enough contiguous acres and the choice is gone.

*Dominant pressures: farm economic resilience, capital discipline. Yielded: some generation, since marginal ground is rarely shaped for output.*

**Cozy Cove Farm, Gurley, Alabama** — a llama-and-alpaca farm that set a 50-kilowatt array on a flood-prone corner of riverside pasture, raised about seven feet so the herd grazes and shelters beneath, selling the power to the TVA while the pasture keeps working. *This particular site reads as [S2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions), not S4: the siting decision was the marginal corner, but production never stopped there — the herd still grazes beneath the panels. It is the archetype's sharing variant, and the reading rule in §2.1 settles it.*

### Solar Prairie Strips {#arch-prairie-strips}


::: {.at-a-glance}
**At a glance** — *indicative: drawn from the worked case and from forms in circulation. Not requirements.*

- **Scale** — A3 · ~1–10 MW · roughly 5–80 acres
- **Position** — S5 — the strip ground leaves production
- **Ground layer** — deep-rooted native prairie, the mix and width sized to a named hydrologic outcome
- **Geometry** — placement follows the water — contour bands, low draws, wet corners, wetland edges
- **Grid** — distribution; often community solar
- **Watch for** — needs a place where clean water is actually paid for; the logic does not carry to utility scale
:::
*Parcel scale [A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · retires impaired ground [S5](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) · restoration by where you plant*

Solar prairie strips have two distinct layers: a strip of prairie that captures water, sediment, and nutrient runoff while providing habitat and biodiversity, and solar panels that anchor the strips — giving them a lasting reason to stay in the ground — while generating power and income for the farmer.

They go in where a field sheds its water: along the contour, down the low draws, around the wet corners, sometimes circling a restored wetland. The panels stand among the grasses rather than over bare or mown ground. Big bluestem, coneflower, and milkweed root deep, holding the soil and slowing the water while the array shares their ground. How much prairie, and where, is a measured decision — enough to soak up a given storm, catch the sediment, keep nitrogen out of the creek. Where runoff must be intercepted the prairie runs in narrow bands across the slope; where a low field or a wetland edge already collects the water, it widens into blocks.

The pattern is not new. It comes from the STRIPS research, which found that converting as little as a tenth of a field to native prairie, set exactly where the water runs, can cut soil loss by more than ninety percent and sharply reduce the nitrogen and phosphorus that leave with it (Schulte et al. 2017). The solar is simply what keeps that patch worth planting. It asks for a place where clean water is paid for, and it does not carry to utility scale, where no one gets to choose the ground.

*Dominant pressures: restorative ambition, social license. Yielded: a little generation, to the prairie.*

**Ramsey Renewable Station, Minnesota** — 3.4 megawatts of solar and storage whose native ground layer is the stormwater system itself: on that sandy soil, DOE's PV-SMaRT modeling found the planting absorbed the 2-, 10-, and 100-year design storms with no detention basins at all.

### Regenerative Solar Grazing {#arch-grazing}


::: {.at-a-glance}
**At a glance** — *indicative: drawn from the worked case and from forms in circulation. Not requirements.*

- **Scale** — A4–A5 · 10 MW and up · from tens of acres to several thousand
- **Position** — S2 — forage production continues, subordinate to the array
- **Ground layer** — managed pasture or forage held under a planned rotation
- **Geometry** — clearance and water points set what class of stock can work beneath; fence and gate topology defines the rotation cells
- **Grid** — sub-transmission to transmission
- **Watch for** — scheduling sovereignty — the plant wants the grass low on its calendar, the shepherd moves stock on the flock's; expect cost parity with mowing, not a saving
:::
*Landscape scale and up [A4–A5](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · shares the ground for grazing [S2](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) · restoration by how it's run*

Regenerative solar grazing has two layers doing complementary work: a flock — usually sheep — that eats the vegetation the array would otherwise pay to mow, and the panels above and among them that make the power. Managed well, the animals are more than a mower on legs; moved across the site on a planned rotation, they trample litter, cycle nutrients, and can leave the soil better than they found it, so the ground cover turns into habitat and the grazing into a small regenerative enterprise.

This is a large-scale practice, and its vegetation is a service rather than the landowner's own farming: a contract grazier brings the flock, the security fence doubles as the paddock, interior fencing and gates lay out the rotation, and clearance height and water points decide what stock can work beneath the modules. The tension is over the calendar — the array wants its grass held low on its own schedule, the shepherd needs to move animals on the flock's, and the regenerative version asks the site to graze for soil and sward health, not only for a tidy sightline. It reaches cost parity with mowing rather than beating it outright, and where the understory is native and well-managed the ground can gain soil carbon over the array's life instead of merely holding steady [@krasner2025].

*Dominant pressures: generation yield, operational simplicity. Yielded: the farm's own agricultural continuity — the grazing is a tenancy, not the operation.*

**Aurora Solar, Minnesota** — 150 megawatts of generation across sixteen sites whose grounds are kept by thousands of contracted sheep grazing a low pollinator understory: vegetation management as a grazing tenancy, at utility scale, rather than the landowner's own farm.

### Water-Sustainability Solar {#arch-water}


::: {.at-a-glance}
**At a glance** — *indicative: drawn from the worked case and from forms in circulation. Not requirements.*

- **Scale** — A4–A5 · 50 MW and up · hundreds to many thousands of acres
- **Position** — S5 — irrigated production ends, by design
- **Ground layer** — low-water cover; the array itself needs no irrigation
- **Geometry** — the unit of design is the district or aquifer, not the parcel
- **Grid** — transmission
- **Watch for** — only works where the overdraft is measured and governed tightly enough that the saved water stays saved
:::
*Landscape scale and up [A4–A5](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · retires impaired irrigated ground [S5](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) · restoration by relieving the water budget*

Water-sustainability solar has two layers in a subtractive relationship: the array, which needs no irrigation, and the aquifer beneath it, which the array is placed to stop draining. Where irrigated farming has been pulling more water than the ground can replace, converting those fields to solar simply ends the demand. The restoration is not something added to the site — it is something that stops happening to the water.

The logic only works where the overdraft is real, measured, and governed. It needs an aquifer stressed enough that retired demand is worth more than the crop, a regulatory regime that makes the saving count rather than letting a neighbour pump it, and ground whose farming was marginal on its own terms — drainage-impaired, salt-affected, or expensive to irrigate — so retirement is not simply taking good land out of food production. That combination is regional rather than scattered, which is why this is the one removal archetype that scales: where a whole district is over its budget there is no cherry-picking to do, and retirement and utility scale stop fighting each other (§2.2). Food production is deliberately let go here, and the archetype should be read as making that trade openly rather than avoiding it.

*Dominant pressures: restorative ambition (a water-quantity target), capital discipline. Yielded: agricultural production, by design.*

**Westlands Solar Park, San Joaquin Valley, California** — part of a plan to convert up to ~136,000 acres of drainage-impaired, previously-irrigated land to solar and storage under California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act; because the panels use no water, retiring the fields eases the overdraft that irrigated farming had driven. *Figures are developer- and program-reported; see [Sources](sources.qmd).*

## Archetypes across the SCALE domains {#sec-archetype-domains}

The six featured archetypes and the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) meet in a matrix: each archetype, by settling its pressures a particular way, produces a characteristic profile across the [SCALE](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-scale) domains — which of Communities, Agriculture, Landscapes, and Energy it foregrounds, and which it trades away. This is the archetype × function matrix read one row at a time.

**How the profiles are derived, so they can be checked.** Each shape is generated from the archetype's own stated pressures by one rule: a **dominant** pressure pushes its domain toward regeneration, a **yielded** pressure pulls its domain toward depletion, and a pressure the archetype does not engage leaves its domain mid-scale. The pressure-to-domain mapping is the one set out in §4: agricultural continuity → Agriculture; restorative ambition and the biophysical functions → Landscapes; social license and the community & economic function → Communities; generation yield, capital discipline and operational simplicity → Energy. Nothing else feeds the shape — no site measurements, no weighting, no aggregate score across domains. That makes each profile reproducible from the text above it and, more importantly, **contestable**: to disagree with a shape, disagree with the pressure reading that produced it. These are judgments about *forms*, not audits of the named projects.

![Each featured archetype as a SCALE footprint across the four domains: a domain it regenerates pulls toward the centre, one it depletes or trades away reaches toward the rim — read from its dominant and yielded pressures. Descriptive profiles, site-conditional — not a ranking and not a score against a limit of sustainability.](../figures/fig_archetype_footprints.svg){#fig-archetypes}

- [**Barnyard Shelter Solar**](#arch-barnyard) (A1 · S1–S2) leans on **Agriculture** (the farm's own animals keep producing) and **Communities** (one operator, behind-the-meter resilience), with **Landscapes** a modest welfare-and-microclimate gain and **Energy** deliberately small — sized to the farm, not the grid.
- [**Vegetable Agrivoltaics**](#arch-vegetable) (A2–A3 · S1) leans on **Agriculture** (food keeps growing in the footprint) and **Communities** (a farmer, a local face), trading **Energy** (the clearance and spacing the crop needs cost generation).
- [**Marginal Land Solar**](#arch-marginal) (A2–A3 · S4, or S2 where grazed) is anchored in **Communities** — the farm's financial resilience — on **Agriculture**'s cast-off ground, with **Energy** cheap to build but modest in yield.
- [**Solar Prairie Strips**](#arch-prairie-strips) (A3 · S5) is a **Landscapes** archetype first — clean water and habitat — with **Communities** benefit visible, yielding some **Energy** to the prairie.
- [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](#arch-grazing) (A4–A5 · S2) foregrounds **Energy** (utility-scale generation) and **Landscapes** (grazed cover, soil, habitat), with **Agriculture** present only as a grazing service, not the farm's own operation.
- [**Water-Sustainability Solar**](#arch-water) (A4–A5 · S5) is a **Landscapes** archetype in the water sense — easing an overdrawn aquifer — deliberately giving up **Agriculture** at the arid end while delivering **Energy** at scale.

No archetype fills every domain, and none is meant to: the profiles differ because the pressures were settled differently. A real project's profile is its own, shaped by site and design; these six are reference shapes, not targets. Whether to overlay the SCALE *limit of sustainability* — turning these descriptive profiles into an evaluation of depletion vs. regeneration — is the call the [metrics open issue](7-open-issues.qmd) (§7, issue 5) leaves deliberately unmade.

## Further archetypes in current circulation {#sec-further-types}

Seven more archetypes, sketched rather than fully developed — the same language applied to configurations the featured six do not cover.

Two of them sit at [S3](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions) despite carrying rich ecological ground layers, and that is not a contradiction: their position records that ordinary ground was given over to the array, while the pollinator planting or restored grassland is a [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) layered on top of it (§2.1, §4).

### Vertical-Bifacial Cropland Array {#arch-vertical-bifacial}

[A2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones)–[A4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S1](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[structure-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* [agricultural continuity](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures), [generation yield](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures).
*Yielded:* [capital discipline](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (frameless glass–glass modules, more posts per watt), land-use density.
*Signature levers:* vertical east–west [module technology](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-module-technology), bifacial modules, wide (~8 m) row geometry set by machinery rather than crop light [@vaverkova2026]. The clean annual-arable S1 case that the overstory geometry misses.

### Community-Solar Pollinator Array {#arch-community-solar}

[A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S3](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[management-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* [social license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures), [restorative ambition](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) with a pollinator/biodiversity service target, [offtake conformity](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (community-solar subscribers plus pollinator/habitat certification as the buying-side channel).
*Yielded:* some [operational simplicity](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) during the multi-year establishment.
*Signature levers:* whole-site native [ground-layer](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer) composition, seeded establishment, mowing/grazing timing set for bloom.

### Native-Grassland Utility Array {#arch-native-grassland}

[A4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones)–[A5](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S3](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[management-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* generation yield, restorative ambition (grassland restoration [@walston2025]).
*Yielded:* agricultural continuity.
*Signature levers:* native seed mix, deferred/rotational mowing, soil-carbon establishment [@krasner2025]. The characteristic large-scale [convergence case](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-wedge) (§2.2).

### Recharge Enhancement Array {#arch-recharge}

[A2](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones)–[A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S4](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[siting-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* [restorative ambition](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (a water-quantity target), farm economic resilience.
*Yielded:* some [generation yield](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (corners are small and awkwardly shaped).
*Signature levers:* placement on ground already out of production where infiltration can be increased — characteristically the dry corners a centre-pivot never reaches — with ground-layer and grading chosen to move rainfall downward rather than off. The supply-side counterpart to [water-sustainability solar](#arch-water): where that one subtracts demand at scale, this one adds recharge on ground already out of production, and the pivot circle keeps farming beside it. **Emerging rather than established** — Kansas Geological Survey, Kansas State, and Michigan State researchers are testing the approach over the Ogallala; it is included as a named pathway to watch, not a documented recurring form.

### Linear Infrastructure Array {#arch-linear}

[A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones)–[A4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S4](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[siting-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* [capital discipline](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (land already disturbed and often already controlled), [social license](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) (prime fields left untouched).
*Yielded:* [generation yield](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) and [operational simplicity](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) — a corridor is a costly shape to build and maintain.
*Signature levers:* placement along highway, rail, pipeline, and transmission easements; mounting specified for the wind and shadow conditions of a corridor; ground layer doubling as verge management. The geometry is the archetype: exceptionally long, narrow bands — a strip a hundred feet wide and a mile long behaves nothing like a block of the same acreage. Its edge-to-area ratio is extreme, which is what makes it interesting for connectivity and hazardous for edge effects (see [influence zone](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-footprint-influence)), and it uses land already fragmented by the infrastructure beside it.

### Ag-Industrial Microgrid Array {#arch-microgrid}

[A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones)–[A4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S3](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)–[S4](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[siting-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* [offtake conformity](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) in its purest form — the load *is* the offtake — and farm economic resilience.
*Yielded:* [restorative ambition](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) on the ground layer, which is rarely the point at an industrial site.
*Signature levers:* siting against a heavy on-farm load — grain drying, cold storage, a feedlot, a processing complex — with battery storage sized to shave peaks, ride through outages, or arbitrage time-of-use rates. It is the one archetype organised around *when* power is used rather than what the ground does, and it is where the [community & economic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) shows up as resilience rather than as rent.

### Brightfield / Reclaimed-Land Array {#arch-brightfield}

[A3](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones)–[A5](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) · **[S4](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-positions)** · *[siting-led](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude)*

*Dominant pressures:* capital discipline (uniformly low-value ground), social license (reuse of degraded land).
*Yielded:* some generation yield (sites are constrained).
*Signature levers:* placement on reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields; remediation constraints on foundations and ground layer. The standing [S4-at-A5 exception](2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd#sec-wedge) (§2.2).

## Associated Terminology {#sec-arch-terms}

Defined here (this section is their collection point):

**Archetype** — A way the [design pressures](3-design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures-ch) have been resolved at a particular scale zone and sharing position; the featured archetypes and further Types above are archetypes, not the object of the lexicon.

**Featured archetype** — one of the six canonical archetypes developed in depth here, in scale order (Barnyard Shelter Solar, Vegetable Agrivoltaics, Marginal Land Solar, Solar Prairie Strips, Regenerative Solar Grazing, Water-Sustainability Solar), each carrying a worked real-world *Application*. A curatorial label, not a claim that these six are more valid than the [further archetypes](#sec-further-types).
